# Git mental model and first repository

::: {.chapter-goals}
**By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:**

- explain the working tree, staging area, repository, commit, branch and
  `HEAD` without calling Git a backup service;
- distinguish untracked, tracked, modified, staged and committed content;
- initialize a repository and create two small, meaningful commits;
- use `git status`, `git diff`, `git diff --staged`, `git log`, `git show` and
  `git ls-files` as evidence;
- design a `.gitignore` without accidentally hiding source or provenance;
- decide which bioinformatics files belong in Git;
- inspect AI-generated changes before accepting them; and
- produce a clean local practice repository that you can explain in an
  interview.
:::

## Why a biologist should care

A computational result depends on more than FASTQ files and a tool name. It
also depends on scripts, workflow definitions, parameters, environment files,
container recipes and decisions that change over time.

Without version control, files often evolve like this:

```text
analysis.sh
analysis_fixed.sh
analysis_final.sh
analysis_final_really.sh
analysis_final_really_2.sh
```

Those names do not answer:

- what changed;
- why it changed;
- who changed it;
- which version produced a result;
- whether two files differ; or
- how to return to a known revision.

Git records deliberate snapshots and the relationships between them. It gives
software changes a reviewable history. It does not decide whether the biology
is correct; it makes the exact analytical instructions available for review.

AI increases the need for this discipline. If an assistant edits eight files,
you need a way to inspect the exact patch, separate useful changes from
unrelated ones and preserve the accepted state.

## Engineering objective

Build this model before memorizing commands:

```text
files you can see and edit
        working tree
             │
             │ git add selects content
             ▼
      staging area / index
             │
             │ git commit records a snapshot
             ▼
     local Git repository
       commits + branches
             │
             │ later: git push
             ▼
      remote repository
       such as GitHub
```

Chapter 6 stops at the local repository. GitHub is introduced in Chapter 8.
This separation matters: Git works without GitHub, and GitHub is not Git.

## Repository, working tree and `.git`

A **repository** is a project whose history Git manages. In a normal local
repository you see the project files plus a hidden `.git` directory:

```text
git-first-repo/
├── .git/            Git's database and local configuration
├── .gitignore       tracked rules for intentionally untracked paths
├── README.md        project explanation
└── workflow.md      example analytical plan
```

The **working tree** is the checked-out collection of ordinary files you edit.
The `.git` directory stores commits, references, configuration and other
metadata. Deleting `.git` does not delete the visible project files, but it
removes that local repository's Git history and identity.

::: {.callout-warning title="Do not edit `.git` by hand"}
Use Git commands to inspect and change repository state. Directly modifying
files inside `.git` can corrupt or misdirect the repository.
:::

## The staging area is a proposed next snapshot

The staging area—also called the **index**—is the content currently selected
for the next commit.

Imagine that you edit `README.md` and `workflow.md`, but only the README is
ready. You can stage only that file:

```bash
git add README.md
```

Now the repository contains three relevant versions:

1. the last committed `README.md`;
2. the staged README proposed for the next commit; and
3. any additional unstaged edits in the working tree.

This is why “I saved the file” and “I committed the change” are different.

## The five file states

| State | Meaning | Useful evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Untracked | File exists but has never been selected for Git | `git status` |
| Tracked and unchanged | Working copy matches the selected commit | clean `git status` |
| Modified | Tracked file differs from the index/commit | `git diff` |
| Staged | Content is selected for the next commit | `git diff --staged` |
| Committed | Snapshot is stored in local history | `git log`, `git show` |

A file can have both staged and unstaged changes. For example, you can stage
one version, edit it again and then see the filename in both sections of
`git status`.

## Commits are snapshots connected by history

A commit records:

- a snapshot of tracked content;
- a reference to its parent commit or commits;
- author and committer information;
- timestamps; and
- a message.

Git identifies a commit using a cryptographic object ID. You often see an
abbreviated form such as:

```text
a17c42e docs: describe the synthetic test fixture
```

Changing commit content or metadata produces a different ID. A commit ID is
therefore more precise than “the latest version,” but an abbreviated ID should
be long enough to remain unique in the repository.

Git is conceptually snapshot-based, even though commands such as `git diff`
show changes between snapshots.

## Branches and `HEAD`

A **branch** is a movable name pointing to a commit. `main` is a common default
branch name. When you create a new commit on `main`, the branch advances to the
new commit.

`HEAD` normally identifies the branch currently checked out:

```text
HEAD ──► main ──► newest commit ──► parent commit
```

This model explains why a branch is cheap: it is primarily a reference, not a
second full copy of every project file.

Branches, switching and merging are developed in Chapter 7. For now, remain on
one local branch and learn to inspect it.

## Git identity is not authentication

Every commit stores an author name and email. Configure them for this practice
repository:

```bash
git config --local user.name "Your Name"
git config --local user.email "you@example.org"
```

`--local` writes configuration for the current repository. It avoids silently
changing every repository on a shared or institutional machine.

Inspect the result:

```bash
git config --local --get user.name
git config --local --get user.email
```

This identity is attribution, not proof that you can access GitHub. SSH keys,
HTTPS tokens and federated login are authentication mechanisms discussed in
Chapter 8.

## What belongs in a bioinformatics repository?

Usually track small, reviewable files that define or explain the analysis:

- Nextflow, Bash, Python or R source;
- `nextflow.config` and nonsensitive parameter examples;
- `environment.yml`, lock files and Dockerfiles;
- small test fixtures when licensing and privacy permit;
- checksum and provenance manifests;
- tests, documentation and diagrams;
- CI/CD workflow definitions; and
- summary evidence small enough to review.

Usually do not track:

- patient or participant data;
- credentials, tokens, private keys or `.env` secrets;
- large FASTQ, BAM, CRAM, index and reference bundles;
- generated result directories;
- Nextflow `work/` and `.nextflow/` state;
- Conda environment directories;
- Docker or Singularity image files; or
- temporary/editor operating-system files.

“Git can store it” is not the same as “Git is the correct governed storage
system for it.”

## `.gitignore` controls untracked discovery

A `.gitignore` file contains patterns for paths Git should normally leave
untracked. A small workflow project might begin with:

```gitignore
# Workflow runtime state
work/
.nextflow/
.nextflow.log*

# Generated data and results
data/
results/
*.bam
*.bai
*.fastq
*.fastq.gz

# Local environments and container artifacts
.conda/
conda-envs/
containers/
*.sif

# Secrets
.env
*.pem
*.key

# Operating-system/editor files
.DS_Store
*~
```

Patterns are project decisions. If `data/` contains a deliberately tiny public
fixture that should be tracked, ignoring the entire directory would be too
broad. You might instead ignore `data/raw/` and explicitly retain
`data/test/mini.fastq`.

Important limitation: `.gitignore` does not make an already tracked file
untracked, remove it from old commits or protect a secret. If a secret entered
history, stop using it, revoke/rotate it and follow your organization's incident
procedure.

Test an ignore decision:

```bash
git check-ignore -v path/to/file
```

This prints the matching rule and its source. No output usually means that path
is not ignored.

## The inspection commands form a safety loop

### `git status`: classify current state

```bash
git status
git status --short
```

The long form teaches what is staged and unstaged. The short form is compact
once you understand the two status columns.

Examples:

```text
?? notes.md       untracked
 M README.md      modified in working tree
M  workflow.md    staged change
MM config.yml     staged content plus additional unstaged edits
```

### `git diff`: inspect unstaged changes

```bash
git diff
git diff -- README.md
```

This compares the working tree with the staging area. It does not show newly
untracked file contents.

### `git diff --staged`: inspect the proposed commit

```bash
git diff --staged
```

This is the final review before `git commit`. If the output contains a key,
patient identifier, large generated file or unrelated edit, do not commit it.

`--cached` is a synonym:

```bash
git diff --cached
```

### `git ls-files`: list what Git tracks

```bash
git ls-files
```

This is more reliable than looking at the directory. A file can exist locally
without being part of the repository.

### `git log` and `git show`: inspect recorded history

```bash
git log --oneline --decorate
git show --stat HEAD
git show HEAD
```

`git log` shows commit history. `git show` displays one commit's metadata and
patch. `HEAD` means the currently selected commit.

## Practical: create your first local repository

This exercise creates a disposable repository with no cloud account, remote or
biological data. Run it somewhere outside another Git repository.

### Step 0 — verify the location

```bash
pwd
git --version
git rev-parse --show-toplevel
```

For the third command, a failure is desirable if you intend to create a new
standalone repository. If it prints an existing parent repository, move to a
different location before continuing.

::: {.callout-warning title="Nested repositories confuse beginners"}
Running `git init` inside an existing repository creates a nested repository.
That can be intentional, but it is not this exercise. Always inspect
`git rev-parse --show-toplevel` first.
:::

### Step 1 — create and initialize the project

```bash
mkdir git-first-repo
cd git-first-repo

git init -b main
git status
```

If an older Git version does not support `-b`, use:

```bash
git init
git branch -M main
```

Confirm the repository root and branch:

```bash
git rev-parse --show-toplevel
git branch --show-current
```

Expected branch: `main`.

### Step 2 — configure repository-local attribution

```bash
git config --local user.name "Your Name"
git config --local user.email "you@example.org"

git config --local --list
```

Use your real professional attribution if this repository will later be
published. The example address is intentionally a placeholder.

### Step 3 — create the initial files

```bash
printf '%s\n' \
  '# Mini workflow engineering lab' \
  '' \
  'A local Git exercise using synthetic data only.' \
  > README.md

printf '%s\n' \
  'work/' \
  'results/' \
  '.nextflow/' \
  '.nextflow.log*' \
  '.env' \
  '*.key' \
  '.DS_Store' \
  > .gitignore
```

Create paths that should be ignored:

```bash
mkdir -p work results
printf 'temporary task state\n' > work/task.txt
printf 'generated output\n' > results/result.txt
```

Inspect:

```bash
git status --short
git check-ignore -v work/task.txt results/result.txt
```

Only `.gitignore` and `README.md` should appear as untracked. The other command
should identify the ignore rules.

### Step 4 — stage and inspect the first snapshot

Stage explicit files:

```bash
git add .gitignore README.md
```

Do not make `git add .` your only habit. It can be appropriate after inspection,
but explicit paths make the intended scope obvious to a beginner.

Review all three views:

```bash
git status
git diff
git diff --staged
```

`git diff` should be empty because there are no unstaged edits. The staged diff
should show the two new files.

### Step 5 — create the first commit

```bash
git commit -m "chore: initialize the learning repository"
```

Verify the result:

```bash
git status
git log --oneline --decorate
git show --stat HEAD
git ls-files
```

The working tree should be clean, and exactly `.gitignore` and `README.md`
should be tracked.

### Step 6 — create a focused second change

Add an analytical plan:

```bash
printf '%s\n' \
  '# Planned workflow' \
  '' \
  '1. Validate paired synthetic FASTQ inputs.' \
  '2. Run read quality control.' \
  '3. Trim adapters and low-quality ends.' \
  '4. Align reads to a declared reference.' \
  '5. Validate the sorted BAM and summarize mapping.' \
  > workflow.md
```

Inspect the state:

```bash
git status --short
git diff
```

`workflow.md` is untracked, so normal `git diff` will not display its content.
Read it directly, then stage it:

```bash
cat workflow.md
git add workflow.md
git diff --staged
```

Commit it:

```bash
git commit -m "docs: add the planned analysis stages"
```

### Step 7 — prove the acceptance conditions

```bash
git status --short
git log --oneline --decorate -2
git ls-files
git show --stat HEAD
git show --stat HEAD~1
```

Acceptance criteria:

- `git status --short` produces no output;
- the log contains two meaningful commits;
- three files are tracked;
- the newest commit contains only `workflow.md`; and
- the first commit contains only `.gitignore` and `README.md`.

Save interview evidence without inventing it:

```bash
{
  printf '%s\n' '=== STATUS ==='
  git status
  printf '%s\n' '=== HISTORY ==='
  git log --oneline --decorate -2
  printf '%s\n' '=== TRACKED FILES ==='
  git ls-files
  printf '%s\n' '=== LATEST COMMIT ==='
  git show --stat --oneline HEAD
} > git-practice-evidence.txt
```

This evidence file is initially untracked. Decide whether it is a useful small
project artifact before adding it; do not automatically create a third commit.

## Read a diff rather than merely looking at colors

A simplified patch looks like this:

```diff
diff --git a/workflow.md b/workflow.md
new file mode 100644
--- /dev/null
+++ b/workflow.md
@@ -0,0 +1,3 @@
+# Planned workflow
+
+1. Validate paired synthetic FASTQ inputs.
```

Interpretation:

- `a/` and `b/` label the compared sides;
- `/dev/null` indicates the file did not exist on the old side;
- `+` lines are additions;
- `-` lines would be removals; and
- the hunk header describes affected line ranges.

Green text is not automatically good and red text is not automatically bad.
Review meaning: a one-line deletion can remove a validation check, and a
hundred-line addition can be generated noise.

## Commit messages are part of the evidence

A useful message completes this sentence:

> If applied, this commit will …

Examples:

```text
docs: record synthetic fixture provenance
fix: fail when paired FASTQ input is incomplete
test: add missing-reference negative case
build: pin samtools container digest
```

Avoid messages such as `stuff`, `changes`, `final`, or `AI update`. The message
should describe the change, not the mood of the author.

A commit should normally represent one coherent reason for change. Small does
not mean one line; it means reviewable and conceptually focused.

## What Git does not guarantee

Git does not automatically prove:

- scientific correctness;
- authenticity of the author's real-world identity;
- compliance with privacy or regulatory policy;
- that an external reference URL still serves the same bytes;
- that ignored data is safely backed up;
- that a remote copy exists;
- that a container or result was built from the commit; or
- that a commit was reviewed.

Those claims need additional controls and evidence: tests, checksums,
provenance, signed artifacts, code review, governed storage and CI/CD.

## Common beginner failures

### “I committed, but my new file is missing”

`git commit` records staged content, not every visible file. Use:

```bash
git status
git ls-files
```

Then stage the intended file and review `git diff --staged`.

### “I added a pattern, but the file is still tracked”

`.gitignore` mainly affects untracked paths. First determine why the file was
tracked and whether removing it from future snapshots is appropriate. Do not
copy an index-removal command without understanding its effect.

### “My result directory disappeared”

Git does not track empty directories, and ignored/generated directories may not
exist in a fresh clone. Scripts should create required output directories.

### “I initialized Git in the wrong directory”

Stop before committing. Inspect:

```bash
pwd
git rev-parse --show-toplevel
git status
```

Do not delete an unexpected `.git` directory until you know whether it contains
valuable history and have confirmed the exact path.

### “Git rejected my commit identity”

Configure a name and email locally, inspect them and retry. This is independent
of GitHub login.

## Reviewing AI-generated Git instructions

AI often proposes commands that produce a desired final state while destroying
useful evidence. Be suspicious of unexplained commands containing:

```text
reset --hard
clean -fd
checkout -- <path>
restore --source ...
push --force
filter-repo
```

These commands have legitimate uses, but they can discard work or rewrite
history. They are not beginner troubleshooting defaults.

Before running any Git command suggested by AI, require answers to:

1. What repository root will it affect?
2. Does it modify the working tree, staging area, commits or remote history?
3. Which exact paths or branches are targeted?
4. Can uncommitted content be lost?
5. Is the operation recoverable, and from what evidence?
6. What read-only command shows the current state first?

Prefer diagnosis with `status`, `diff`, `log`, `show`, `branch` and
`rev-parse` before mutation.

## Hands-on exercise: audit an AI-authored change

In your practice repository, ask an AI system to propose one paragraph for the
README explaining why synthetic data is used. Do not let it commit for you.

Then:

1. inspect `git status --short`;
2. inspect the unstaged patch with `git diff`;
3. check the text for claims the project does not demonstrate;
4. edit or reject unsupported claims;
5. stage only `README.md`;
6. inspect `git diff --staged`;
7. write a commit message describing your accepted change; and
8. prove the final working tree is clean.

Create `ai-change-review.md` outside the practice repository or leave it
untracked. Record:

```markdown
# AI change review

## Requested change
## Files the AI proposed changing
## Claims independently verified
## Claims corrected or rejected
## Final staged scope
## Commit ID
## Post-commit status
```

The important skill is not producing the paragraph. It is controlling scope,
validating meaning and establishing traceable acceptance.

## Ten interview questions

### 1. What is the difference between the working tree, staging area and repository?

<details><summary>Model answer</summary>

The working tree contains the files currently checked out for editing. The
staging area holds the exact content proposed for the next commit. The local
repository stores commits, references and history under `.git`. Saving, staging
and committing are therefore three different state transitions.

</details>

### 2. Why can `git diff` be empty when `git status` shows a new file?

<details><summary>Model answer</summary>

Normal `git diff` compares tracked working-tree content with the index. An
untracked file has no indexed version to compare, so its content is not shown.
I inspect the file directly, stage it intentionally and then use
`git diff --staged`.

</details>

### 3. What does `git add` actually do?

<details><summary>Model answer</summary>

It copies the selected content into the index as part of the proposed next
snapshot. It does not create a commit, upload anything to GitHub or permanently
save all future edits to that file.

</details>

### 4. Is a Git commit a diff or a snapshot?

<details><summary>Model answer</summary>

Git's model is snapshot-based: a commit refers to a complete tree of recorded
content plus metadata and parent relationships. Git efficiently stores and
displays differences, which is why users often experience commits as patches.

</details>

### 5. What is a branch, and what does `HEAD` mean?

<details><summary>Model answer</summary>

A branch is a movable reference to a commit. `HEAD` normally identifies the
currently checked-out branch, which in turn points to the current commit. A new
commit advances that branch reference.

</details>

### 6. Why is `.gitignore` not a security control?

<details><summary>Model answer</summary>

It only influences which untracked paths Git normally reports or stages. It
does not encrypt files, prevent another program from reading them, remove
already tracked content or erase old commits. Exposed credentials must be
revoked or rotated even if an ignore rule is later added.

</details>

### 7. Which bioinformatics artifacts would you track, and which would you exclude?

<details><summary>Model answer</summary>

I track reviewable source, configuration, environment/container specifications,
tests, documentation, provenance and small permitted fixtures. I exclude
sensitive data, secrets, large raw/generated files, workflow caches, local
environments and container binaries. Exact choices follow governance,
licensing, reproducibility and repository-size requirements.

</details>

### 8. Does a clean working tree prove the analysis is reproducible?

<details><summary>Model answer</summary>

No. It only says tracked working-tree and staged content match the selected
commit and there are no reported untracked changes. Reproducibility also needs
inputs, dependencies, parameters, runtime, references, provenance and
validation evidence.

</details>

### 9. How would you verify what a commit contains before sharing it?

<details><summary>Model answer</summary>

Before committing I use `git status` and `git diff --staged`. After committing I
use `git show --stat <commit>` for scope and `git show <commit>` for the patch,
plus `git ls-files` when tracked-file inventory matters. I also scan for
secrets, sensitive data and unintended generated files.

</details>

### 10. Why should an AI not automatically stage and commit every change it generates?

<details><summary>Model answer</summary>

Generation is not review. The AI may change unrelated files, include secrets,
invent claims, misunderstand repository policy or bundle several concerns. A
human or authorized review process should inspect the patch, test behavior,
control staged scope and choose a message that accurately records the accepted
change.

</details>

## What you should now be able to explain

You should be able to point to any visible project file and say whether Git is
ignoring it, tracking it, staging a change or storing it in a commit. You should
also be able to prove that your first repository contains two deliberate
snapshots and no unexplained working-tree changes.

The next chapter turns this static model into a safe daily workflow using
branches, focused commits, comparisons, restoration and merge-conflict
reasoning.
